content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents an experimental design for evaluating the effects of augmentation, multiple cropping, and types of learning on the accuracy of a classification task between control and drug treatment of cell lines from grayscale image collections. The type of CNN classification architectures include weakly-supervised, self-supervised, regularized, and unsupervised learning of image representations. 
The experimental evaluations are performed using feature distance, classification model accuracy, and clustering metrics over 16 deep learning training setups on the 770k image dataset under identical conditions.
The novelty of the work is in performing the experimental design, evaluating the metrics, and drawing conclusions about setups and classification accuracy.
content.main_review:
Strength: 
The authors report an interesting experimental design study that includes four types of model architectures, augmentation, and multicrop while evaluating the representation power via feature distance, classification model accuracy, and clustering metrics.

Weakness:
The authors should provide deeper insights into the experimental design and explain the factors of the experimental design. For example, the authors can explain how adding the multicrop option with 1, ½, and ¼ resized crops is expected to introduce model invariance to size variations as a function of spatial resolution. Similarly, adding augmentations into the training data that include, for instance, Gaussian blur, will introduce higher robustness of the ai model to out-of-focus images. On the other hand, introducing multicrop and Gaussian blur might decrease classification accuracy while increasing generalizability and avoiding overfitting the training data. 

The authors should provide similar insights about the model types (i.e., unsupervised, self-supervised, weakly-supervised, and regularized learning of image representations) in Section 4.1 so that the reader understands the reasoning behind selecting the model types and the expectations from each model architecture before the results are presented. 

The Table 2 would also benefit from reporting standard deviations to understand the confidence intervals for each accuracy measurement.

Minor comments:
The authors could also claim a contribution in assembling an evaluation dataset with semantically meaningful labels (i.e., MTX, PTX, and DMSO labels) assuming that the authors would share the dataset with the community. Others could reuse the dataset for other evaluation studies. 
Is there a conflict in the claims that all models have been trained with the same set of hyper-parameters”
•	Section 4.2: “We trained all models on the same dataset for 50 epochs, using Adam optimizer with a constant learning rate of 0.0001. A batch size of 256 was used”
•	Section 4.3.2: “We used the same data splits for all models and trained them for 25 epochs with SGD optimizer and batch size of 1024”
•	Section 7: “We used the same optimizers, batch sizes and other training parameters to ensure fair comparison of learned representations”
content.summary_of_the_review:
Summary statement:
The paper is well written, and the technical part is clearly presented. I am missing a bit more insights about the experimental design and statistical confidence in the accuracy measurements (and hence derived conclusions).

content.title: More details on study design
content.comment:
__Augmentations and multi-crops__

Design of augmentations and multi-crops was driven by our aspiration to learn unbiased representative features of the cells. We had around 20 cell lines in the dataset and multiple time points capturing the process of cells’ growth under drug treatment. The size and shape of individual cells varied largely (e.g., approximately 5x5 pixels for one cell type and 6x25 pixels for another). Furthermore, the density of growing cell populations and their prevalent location on the crop also varied a lot. We introduced augmentations and random resized crops of 1/2 and 1/4 of initial image size to encourage models to learn more complex features rather than cell locations, sizes or population densities. However, using more crops requires times more computations, that’s why we used 5 multi-crops at max to be able to train within reasonable time. Introducing Gaussian blur was important to cope with microscopy visual aberrations sometimes appearing on the crops.

__Model types__

The choice of training approaches and model types is motivated by a number of recent applications, discussed in the related work section. Similar models had been used extensively in the field, though fair comparison of learned representations was missing. We intended to fill this gap, inspire and inform future applications.

__Evaluation__

- The reviewer noted that __Table 2__ would benefit from reporting standard deviations. We find this suggestion very helpful. We will provide median absolute deviations for the median statistics in __Table 2__ in rebuttal revision.
- We did not disclose details about the dataset, because another publication for a high-impact biological journal is being prepared. The data will be published and made openly available for other researchers.
- There is no contradiction in the claims cited by the reviewer in "minor comments" section. Hyper-parameters differed between training and evaluation setups, but they were identical across models within those two setups. Therefore, the comparison of learned representations was not affected.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents empirical results on the efficacy of convolutional neural networks when applied to three down-stream tasks using a gray-scale, image dataset of drug-treated, in vitro cancer cell populations. Specifically, this paper compares the performance of four different CNN models using an identical “base” layer stack with varying training approaches (categorical cross-entropy, auto-encoder, auto-encoder with regularization, and self-supervised). For each combination, the authors compare performance when trained with and without random augmentations and with and without multiple image crops.

Each of the four models are trained using the same dataset, but with a problem setup appropriate for the particular model. To standardize the evaluation of models trained using differing problem setups, the “base” layer stack which is identical for all models is extracted and used to generate latent representations of hold-out images. These representations are then evaluated using multiple tasks: distance in latent representation for known drugs, classification of cells treated with a drug or control, and clustering performance of various cell lines.

The papers primary contributions:
* Comparing the usefulness of latent representations for downstream tasks obtained from four different CNN modeling approaches on the same biological image dataset
* Comparing the effect of applying random augmentations and multiple image crops  on downstream performance
content.main_review:
## Motivation
The application of machine learning, and specifically CNNs, to biological image data is interesting and well motivated. Improvements in this domain can offer significant benefits to society and past work in this area has led to interesting machine learning contributions (e.g. the U-Net). Additionally, rigorous empirical analysis of machine learning models applied to many scientific domains, including biology, is often limited so works that focus on this can be useful to other researchers working in this domain.

## Strengths
This paper uses a common dataset for model evaluation which is useful for comparing the various approaches investigated. Many other papers in this area only adopt a single modeling approach and each paper utilizes different datasets so direct comparison of methods is difficult or impossible.

This paper utilizes a common “base” layer stack in all of it’s approaches and uses this common layer stack for it’s feature extraction. This helps simplify comparison between the different methods examined.

This paper explores three different down-stream tasks using the same dataset. This is useful to help identify if specific models perform best broadly, or only on a specific task. 

This paper follows the page limit and is easy to follow and understand.

## Weaknesses
This paper uses a relatively small CNN for it’s experiments (the base layer stack consists of only three layers with 64, 32, and 8 filters in each, respectively). Significantly larger models are often used in this domain and the results of this paper may change with larger models. If models of various overall sizes were compared and the results found to be similar this would be worth reporting. It is possible that the limited computational resources (a single RTX 2060) may have factored into the model size used.

This paper does not explore other, common architecture features or designs (e.g. multi-scale CNNs, residual connections) which are often used in image and video CNN models. These, and other methods, have shown significant value both within the biology domain and more broadly. 

This paper only utilizes a single dataset for evaluation. While the use of multiple down-stream tasks for the dataset is positive, in order for the paper to demonstrate more generalizable results for machine learning practitioners working in this domain the use of several biological image datasets is important. There may be specific aspects of the chosen dataset that affect the comparison of the different models.

The finding that multi-crops and random augmentations generally improve performance in downstream tasks is not unexpected. While this is not problematic, this is not a significant contribution.

The paper does not present any significant, specific results that are actionable for other machine learning practitioners or researchers in this domain. The performance of the models vary between downstream tasks and the models often perform similarly. From the last line of the paper, “no single combination of model (architecture) and setting (augmenting and cropping strategies) consistently outperformed the others.”  

The paper does not present any novel methods or techniques beyond its empirical results.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is well motivated. It explores an interesting and valuable domain and papers that perform empirical evaluations and comparisons of relevant machine learning models can be useful for practitioners and researchers. 

However, empirical studies need strong evaluations as the experiments are the primary contribution. Such studies should strive to be generalizable and present useful findings to maximize their impact. This paper is marginal in both of these areas. 

For this paper to make well-supported, generalizable statements it needs to investigate larger models with a greater variety of architectural compositions. It should evaluate at least one other dataset to ensure its findings are not specific to the specific dataset chosen. And a larger variety of experiments should be performed (multiple random initializations for each model with reported variance, a variety of hyper-parameter settings with discussion on the sensitivity of the results to them). 

For this paper to present more useful findings it should present results that are either extremely strong (e.g. a certain model consistently and significantly outperforms others) or surprising (e.g. a commonly used technique or model has key limitations). Here the paper presents generally unclear results (with respect to which modeling approach performs best) and unsurprising results (that random augmentation and multi-crops improve performance).

display_title: Machine learning within limited resources is important. We train and evaluate on a huge heterogeneous dataset. We actually present novel and actionable empirical findings

content.title: Machine learning within limited resources is important. We train and evaluate on a huge heterogeneous dataset. We actually present novel and actionable empirical findings
content.comment:
__Study design__

Using a single RTX 2060 with 6 GB, indeed, shaped the design of this study (layers, filters, architecture features, etc.). However, we do not see it as weakness. The paper targets both machine learning and life science communities, where researchers do not often have access to computational clusters with top performing GPU/TPUs. They can directly benefit from our empirical findings and inform their own study design. Besides, future comparative studies (e.g., with larger networks, as the reviewer proposed) can refer to ours to improve and better generalise results. As the reviewer pointed out, there is very few similar papers, because the comparison is difficult or sometimes impossible. This adds value to our work.

__Evaluation__

Using multiple datasets instead of one would, indeed, lead to more generalisable results. On the other hand, it is rare that a dataset of 770k biological images is used for systematic evaluation of different machine learning models. The dataset we worked with covers over 30 drugs at 5 different concentrations applied to over 20 cell lines along the time axis. This is a large and highly heterogeneous dataset, which suggests more reliable comparison results compared to some other [studies](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.13122.pdf) using [60 times smaller](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1902.03368.pdf) biological datasets. We did not disclose more details about our data, because another biological publication is being prepared, where the data will be explained and made openly available.

__Actionable results__

The fact that the results among models are comparable speaks for reproducibility and robustness of the evaluation. However, we find the following two empirical findings directly actionable: _i)_ the regularized model produced the best performance across tasks, _ii)_ the self-supervised model resulted in competitive performance requiring 6-11 times less training time, which was _rather surprising_. Although not pronounced in the main text, this implies the future research should definitely explore a combination of these models for applications (e.g., the same BYOL formulation with domain-specific regularization) to benefit from both, training efficiency and quality of representations. We’ll update the main text to better communicate this point.

content.title: Response to Author Comments
content.comment:
Thank you for your response and alterations to the paper. 

**Study Design**

Indeed, many researchers do not have access to large quantities of top-performing GPUs or TPUs. However, for an empirical paper, it is crucial to explore the effect of model size on performance as deeper models can significantly change the performance of architectures on some problems. Of course, it should not be a strict requirement that all researchers have access to a large amount of computing power. This can be exclusionary and may lead to over-emphasizing results that are not as relevant to domain researchers with limited resources. Nevertheless, I believe it is important to explore the role of model size on the performance of the architectures to determine if further experimentation with deeper models is warranted. Such an exploration could include adding and removing layers, changing the number of kernels in each layer, "stretching" the model by adding layers and reducing the number of kernels in each layer, or training larger models and taking advantage of certain techniques (such as checkpointing or fp16) to fit within the GPU memory budget. Even limited experiments here may be sufficient to identify if deeper or larger models need to be studied in greater depth.

**Evaluation**

It can be time-consuming and resource-intensive to process and train with multiple datasets; however, doing so is vital to determine if the results you find can be generalized to a larger class of problems. The fact that the dataset used is quite large is relevant but does not guarantee that the findings are not specific to the dataset. 

**Actionable Results**

Yes, I like the idea of better emphasizing the specific, actionable results and suggestions for future research directions.

**Summary**

The paper contributes valuably to the ongoing study of machine learning methods in the medical image domain. However, without more extensive and robust experiments, strongly supported and surprising findings that would inform future research, or novel contributions to the broader machine learning community, I don't think that this paper is well-suited for the general ICLR ML audience. Perhaps a more domain-focused, machine learning conference or journal is a more appropriate venue.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2452 by Reviewer A2j6

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents an empirical evaluation of representation learning strategies for cellular image analysis. The application domain is drug screening where cancer cells are exposed to different drugs and then microscopy images are captured to detect their effects. There is no ground truth for this type of biological experiment, because the goal is to reveal drug activity and efficacy rather than classifying known patterns. The paper evaluates 4 models under 4 experimental configurations and the results are reported and discussed.
content.main_review:
The paper is well written and discusses previous research in the field extensively.

Dataset: The images come from brightfield microscopy without fluorescent stains. The total number of perturbations is above 600, which is representative from most drug screens. There are also several cell lines and time points available to evaluate the efficacy of compounds.
* It is unclear why the study takes 770k images of 64x64 pixels, when presumably the original microscopy fields of view are larger. Are these random crops or cell segmentation is performed?
* The paper says that single crops are full images resized to a fixed size, while multiple crops are 4 random crops taken from the original image. Is the base for cropping the set of 770k 64x64 images?

Models: the study is focused on training a convolutional network as a feature extractor. The convnet is trained with 4 different strategies: WSL (weakly supervised learning), AE (autoencoders), SSL (self-supervised learning) and RegL (regularized learning). These models are the major strategies for representation learning, and it is interesting to compare them in this domain.
* Is the common convnet encoder a three layer convnet as depicted in Figure 2? This is a simple architecture that can be run efficiently, but may not be the best to capture image features. Other architectures such as small ResNets could have a slightly higher computational cost while obtaining better performance.
* Representation learning is usually evaluated using a linear classification regime, but in this case, the authors chose to use a two layer classifier. This further indicates that the original architecture lacks capacity for disentangling representations and additional non-linearities are needed to recognize patterns.

Evaluation tasks: there are three tasks where the representation learning aspects are evaluated, 1) the distance between MTX, PTX and DMSO; 2) the binary classification of treated vs untreated cells; and 3) clustering. With more than 600 compounds, multiple cell lines and multiple time points, the dataset could have been to perform other interesting analysis / evaluations.
* The Euclidean distance in the first test may not be the optimal metric to compare these samples. The cosine similarity or Pearson correlation could yield different results. 
* A binary classification task between treatments and controls should not need supervision (with a two-layer classifier) if the representation is powerful enough. This separation would be expected in an unsupervised way. More interestingly, the separation could be measured for each compound individually and report how many of the 600 compounds can be tell apart from DMSO (with some distance or statistical threshold).
* Clustering can result in an arbitrary measure, unless clusters correspond with some biologically meaningful group of compounds. With 600 compounds, some of them may have known connections (such as MTX and PTX) that could be used to evaluate if they appear close by in similar groups.

Results: Among all models and configurations tested, it is still hard to identify a strategy that could be used to scale drug screening effectively. The relative performance according to the three selected tasks is almost similar, and beyond computational efficiency, there is no real insight into what could be the future of analyzing these images. The chosen metrics and the way the results are presented do not convey a clarifying message on how to approach the problem presented here. The paper presents concluding remarks that are in line with observations from prior work, and it's hard to identify what is the message or recommendation.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a systematic evaluation of representation learning approaches applied to cellular images for drug screening. The tasks selected for evaluation seem weak and the results do not clearly illuminate a way forward. The models could be improved in terms of learning capacity, and the metrics could be extended to provide more insights into what makes a difference for drug discovery.

content.title: Based on our empirical findings, the most promising strategy to scale drug screening is a combination of self-supervised (efficient, label-free) and regularized (maintaining properties of the data) learning
content.comment:
__Dataset__

- We subset the initial high-resolution 1.1M image dataset to 770k image dataset of 64x64 crops for two reasons: _i)_ to be able to formulate a balanced binary classification problem (drug vs control), which was important to cover the weakly-supervised setting in learning representations and model evaluation (classification task); _ii)_ to be able to train all models within limited resources (we used a single Nvidia GeForce RTX 2060 with 6 GB only; larger crops usually require more memory).
- Augmentations and random resized crops were performed on the 64x64 crops. So, indeed, single crops were the crops themselves, while four additional ones were cropped at different scales from 64x64s and then randomly augmented. We will try to make it clearer in the main text with rebuttal revision.

__Models__

- Our empirical findings (__Table 2__) suggest that the common CNN backbone managed to capture image features relevant for downstream tasks well. Although we do not provide details, we tested >10 other architectures keeping the total number of layers and parameters low to be able to train all models within limited resources. In the paper we presented and evaluated the best performing CNN backbone across training tasks. Retrospectively, we can explain the best performance of this backbone by balancing a large receptive field (maps of 16x16 in the bottleneck layer with 3x3 convolutions, while the full crops are 64x64) and a high reconstruction quality (examples are given in supplementary materials).
- The comparison we presented was done across different machine learning paradigms. While we probably could train a small ResNet to address binary classification, we would not be able to use it as a common backbone to address reconstruction problem with encoder-decoder architecture. Certainly not within limited resources.
- The classification with two linear layers was done to explore the capabilities of the self-supervised model, but keep the comparison fair. The self-supervised model was the fastest to train, produced rather competitive results on clustering task and distance-based analysis, however, it performed poorly on the classification task using only a single linear layer. We hypothesised that with combinations of features allowed by the two consequent linear layers, the classification results would be much closer to the best models. The hypothesis was driven by the general observation that self-supervised approaches (such as BYOL, SwAV, DINO) tend to learn more general features. However, it did not hold, as the __Table 2__ shows.

__Evaluation__

- Several comments made by the reviewer were based on a misunderstanding. We’re sorry about this and we'll try to improve the wording to make it clearer. We did not have over 600 drugs or chemical compounds to alter morphology of the cells. We had around 20 cell lines and 30 drugs tested on several concentrations each. Altogether it makes 693 unique combinations mentioned in the text. We did not disclose more details about the data, because another biological publication is being prepared, where the dataset will be explained and made openly available.
- We tested several metrics in distance-based analysis. The results we reported were consistent for Euclidean and Bray-Curtis distances. Cosine similarity and correlation distance did not produce any significant differences between control and drug images across all models.

__Results__

- The fact that the results among models are comparable speaks for reproducibility and robustness of the evaluation. Still, we have shown a great potential for using the self-supervised models: they produce informative representations, require no labelling and are the fastest to train. This empirical finding is important and shaping future applications.
- The reviewer pointed out that we did not pronounce any recommendation for the future research. We acknowledge it is a simple, yet an important outcome for a paper like ours. We have shown that regularized learning produces the best performance across tasks. However, it was also the most demanding it terms of memory and computation. In contrast to that, the self-supervised paradigm resulted in competitive performance requiring 6-11 times less training time, which was not at all expected. Therefore, we see the future in combination of these approaches: self-supervised problem setting, regularized to maintain certain properties of the data coming from the domain knowledge. We’ll try to fit this in the main text with rebuttal revision.

content.title: Benchmark data and backbone model need to be improved
content.comment:
Thanks to the authors for clarifying these questions.

The following two critical issues still represent major weaknesses of this submission:
1) Dataset. There are several publicly available datasets that can be used to evaluate the research questions presented in this paper. It would have been more valuable to the community if at least some of these datasets is reused as a primary benchmark or as an additional evaluation. This is specially important for reproducibility and for making the results of widespread utility instead of being specific to the data that the authors own.
2) The backbone model may not capture enough visual variation. It is unclear if other architectural innovations developed recently could help solving these tasks with higher accuracy. If computation is an issue, just comparing a ResNet trained with weakly supervised learning vs BYOL would have been much more informative. ResNet18 is a small and efficient model, and it has been used to train decoders as well (e.g. the Cellpose segmentation model). It's not quite conclusive how the training strategies can help when the model does not have enough learning capacity.

For these reasons, after reading the comments of other reviewers, and after careful consideration, I decided to change the recommendation to reject.

content.title: There is no evidence against the proposed backbone model
content.comment:
We also thank the reviewer for a discussion and add a few additional comments.

__Backbone__

The fact that there may be more powerful models out there does not mean the proposed model does not have enough learning capacity. There is no evidence for that. Conversely, the empirical results we obtained throughout the study indicate that the proposed CNN backbone was capable of learning relevant representations (for distance-based analysis of known drugs and for drug-vs-control classification task) under multiple machine learning setups. Moreover, we have yet another evidence supporting sufficient learning capability of the proposed architecture.

As additional validation of the proposed CNN backbone architecture, we compared the unsupervised learning setup with a pretrained ResNet-50 to classify drugs versus controls (in a transfer learning scenario). There, we followed a classical linear evaluation protocol with a single linear layer on top of latent representations. The unsupervised model with similar 3-layer encoder architecture now trained on 128x128 crops delivered 0.81 median accuracy, whereas ResNet-50 in a transfer learning setting reached only 0.61 median accuracy. It might be true that ResNet-50 could beat our architecture if trained on the same data from scratch. But it still indicates the proposed CNN backbone architecture has enough learning capacity.

__Dataset__

We acknowledge that having multiple datasets would only strengthen our results. However, we'd like to draw the reviewer's attention to the fact, that some datasets are worth a dozen when it comes to the size, heterogeneity, etc. Although not yet published, our dataset is at least order of magnitude larger than other biological datasets and covers much more biological variance. Therefore, our findings should generalise way better for future biological applications than many previous works.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors compare representation learning pipelines for biological images on three downstream tasks. They combine four different architectures with absence/presence of two data augmentation strategies, producing a total of 16 different representation learning settings. The settings are evaluated on three downstream tasks: (i) distances of similar compounds, (ii) binary classification and (iii) clustering.
content.main_review:
The question which the authors have decided to tackle is an interesting one: is it possible to identify a representation learning method that performs better for a certain number of common downstream tasks, when it comes to biological microscopy images? However, the paper is (1) too limited in scope, and (2) fails to convey a convincing response to that question on the ground it chose. 

(1) To produce general results for Bioimage informatics, it would be interesting to include other types of images such as fluorescence images, and discuss how certain approaches might work for fluorescence microscopy and not brightfield, and vice versa. It would also be interesting to investigate along the cell line axis, for example how do representations learned on most cell lines generalize on others on average? Is a given method better at transfer learning across cell lines? Across types of imaging (fluorescence vs. brightfield)?

(2) Major comments:
- Data: from section 3 “some drugs did not provoke any effect on resistant cell lines, so the corresponding images of drugs and controls look the same”. This is problematic, both for architecture (a) and downstream task (ii): it will be difficult to get signals from a binary classification task if the dataset is noisy, i.e. not all datapoints in the “drug” class actually belong to it. Indeed, even if cells have been exposed to a drug, if they’re not significantly different from controls, then the images belong to the control class. Furthermore, no data quality control is mentioned, the data does not seem to be from a public dataset and there is no detailed data description.
- Evaluation and results: 
    - The distance evaluation is performed on a single pair of similar known drugs. As such, this result is too limited to conclude whether a given approach produced a biologically meaningful space. Are there other drugs in the set that one expects to be close? Maybe drugs with a common mode-of-action? Or cell lines from a common tissue?
    - The clustering evaluation is not presented in a way that can be used to evaluate learned representations, because there is no groundtruth. If there is no known cluster structure in the problem (e.g. drug classes), why would the best method be the one to find clusters?
    - Standard deviations are not provided for any of the results. As such, it is not possible to evaluate the numbers which are provided either in figure 3, 4 or table 2. Providing standard deviations is all the more important when working with biological data, as there can be large variations between images of cells from the same cell line exposed to the same drug. For example in the case of the binary classification evaluation, cross-validation should be performed, and both the average and the standard deviation of classification accuracy over folds should be indicated.
    - The training code is not provided, just the architectures.

Minor comments:
- Data:
    - The 770k dataset cannot be referred as such in the abstract or intro, as it seems to be an in-house dataset (no publication is cited and Google does not easily locate it). If the dataset is new, this should be made clear, and data description should be like in an article for a biological journal (it can go in the Appendix if it is too long). For example how long were the cells exposed for prior to image acquisition? Which cell lines were included? How many batches, replicates? Any quality control, e.g. for images with low cell count? Any correction for batch effect?
    - If a statistical test is performed to detect which highest dose drugs are not active, it can also be used to detect which lower dose drugs are. This would enrich the dataset by making it possible to include images from other than the highest dose exposure.
- Experimental settings:
    - Why BYOL and another self-supervised method?
    - It is surprising that the binary classifier architecture (a) has a two-dimensional output.
    - The training setups are not very clear.
    - “We chose the CNN backbone architecture, batch size and other common hyperparameters by running grid search” It would be better to specify what set of hyper-parameters were tested during the grid search.
    - “In many cases, we encountered a cuda-out-of-memory runtime error, which was connected to the higher dimensionality of the projection layer, compared to the hidden layer”. This error should be fixed, or the parameter range that raises this error not considered as tested - rather than be in the body of the article.
- Figures: it will be clearer to read if there is one subplot per cell line, rather than one per pipeline. As such, one can mostly see that some cell lines are easier than others to deal with for a certain task.
- Other: limit the use of terms such as “AI”. Also prefer to use the term “learned representations” or “latent representations” rather than “codes” (multiple uses p.5-6)
content.summary_of_the_review: The question which the authors have decided to tackle is an interesting one: is it possible to identify a representation learning method that performs better for a certain number of common downstream tasks, when it comes to biological microscopy images? However, the paper is (1) too limited in scope, and (2) fails to convey a convincing response to that question on the ground it chose.

content.title: We address representation learning of a large specific dataset rather broadly and within limited resources, which targets both machine learning and life science communities
content.comment:
__Scope__

There are many interesting biological questions one could pose and investigate using deep representation learning. However, those would be of little interest to the machine learning community. Comparisons of transfer learning scenarios across cell lines and types of imaging proposed by the reviewer would be amazing biological applications, but certainly irrelevant for a machine learning conference paper. We tried to address the representation learning of a large specific dataset rather broadly and within limited resources, which we believe targets both machine learning and life science communities.

__Data__

- The reviewer mentioned that architecture (a) may be problematic for drug vs control classification in case when some drugs do not show any effect. We believe this could, indeed, be problematic for a clinical application, but not for the comparison of learned representations, since the evaluation setups were identical for all models. Furthermore, the only way to resolve this issue is to label all the data manually using expert knowledge, instead of automated weak-labelling. This would be very demanding given the size of the dataset and also prone to introducing other types of noise and biases. To our knowledge, the noise in drug-control weak labelling was not substantial, which was also supported by comparable performance of the weakly-supervised and the unsupervised models in the classification task.
- We do not disclose details about the dataset, because another publication for a high-impact biological journal is being prepared. The data will be published and made openly available.  

__Evaluation and results__

- A single pair of drugs (PTX and MTX) used for distance-based analysis is the only example we made and, to our knowledge, the best possible example for this dataset. We discussed the limitation of using a single pair in the main text. However, not using any a-priori knowledge about the drugs to validate and compare representations would be a strong disadvantage. And using more examples would make the results controversial, due to the need to motivate the fairness of comparisons of different pairs of drugs. Meanwhile, comparison of PTX and MTX was already the ground of journal publications (cited in the main text) and is, therefore, undoubtedly valid. However, extensive comparison of any drugs is beyond the scope of our work.
- The reviewer referred to the fundamental challenge of evaluating clustering results and expressed concerns about using clustering to compare representations. We believe, however, that comparing measures reflecting the properties of obtained partitions is reasonable, since the data and all the task conditions were kept the same. The only differences we observed are, therefore, due different representation learning approaches. We include number of clusters and percent of noise points, because these reflect how much "structure" the learned representations provide. We had more than 30 drugs in the dataset, so one could expect as many clusters within each cell line. Meanwhile, the weakly-supervised model produced 19 clusters on average and the regularized model produced only 6. These results suggest the regularized model delivered more conservative representations, and the weakly-supervised model captured drug effect patterns better (also supported by the consistently higher recall in the classification task, see Table 2), which are two novel empirical findings.
- We agree that providing deviation measures is important for analysis of biological data and find this comment very useful. We’ll provide median absolute deviations for Table 2 in rebuttal revision.
- We’ll also provide the source code according to the ICLR code submission guidelines to ensure reproducibility of results.

__Experimental settings__

- We chose BYOL, because it is one of the state-of-the-art self-supervised algorithms, efficient and easy to implement. Besides, we could successfully train a CNN backbone using BYOL within limited resources. For instance, we could not train DINO using the same Nvidia GeForce RTX 2060 with 6 GB only.
- Using higher projection layer dimensionality in BYOL could not in principle be fixed, as the reviewer suggested, because it was caused by a fundamental limitation of the hardware (memory).
- We implemented 16 frequently used model setups, including state-of-the-art self-supervised learning, trained them within limited resources and systematically compared latent representations. We find this empirical result very useful for the broad scientific community today.
